claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Aydogan et al., 2020 and is illustrated in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Centrioles are cytoskeletal organelles that form centrosomes, the major microtubule organizing centers (MTOCs) that aid the assembly of mitotic spindles in dividing cells.
claims.source: Centrioles are cytoskeletal organelles that form centrosomes – the major microtubule organizing centers (MTOCs) that aid the assembly of mitotic spindles in dividing cells (reviewed in Banterle and Gönczy, 2017; Conduit et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to review articles by Banterle and Gönczy, 2017 and Conduit et al., 2015.

claims.claim: In most cycling systems, older centrioles (mothers) act as a platform where new centrioles (daughters) start assembling orthogonally.
claims.source: In most cycling systems, older centrioles (i.e., the mothers) act as a platform where new centrioles (i.e., the daughters) start assembling orthogonally (Breslow and Holland, 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Breslow and Holland, 2019.

claims.claim: Polo-like kinase 4 (Plk4) is an enzyme essential for the formation of centrioles.
claims.source: Polo-like kinase 4 (Plk4), an enzyme essential for the formation of centrioles, determines the exact site of daughter centriole assembly on the mothers (Kim et al., 2013; Ohta et al., 2014; Sonnen et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2013; Ohta et al., 2014; and Sonnen et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Plk4 determines the exact site of daughter centriole assembly on the mother centrioles.
claims.source: Polo-like kinase 4 (Plk4), an enzyme essential for the formation of centrioles, determines the exact site of daughter centriole assembly on the mothers (Kim et al., 2013; Ohta et al., 2014; Sonnen et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2013; Ohta et al., 2014; and Sonnen et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Plk4 localizes to centrioles in an oscillatory manner and appears to determine an effective enzymatic threshold that initiates and times centriole biogenesis.
claims.source: Recent work has shown that Plk4 localizes to centrioles in an oscillatory manner and appears to determine an effective enzymatic threshold that initiates and times centriole biogenesis (Aydogan et al., 2020; Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Aydogan et al., 2020 and is illustrated in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The adaptive nature of Plk4 oscillations helps to provide homeostasis for centriole growth in fly embryos.
claims.source: The adaptive nature of Plk4 oscillations helps to provide homeostasis for centriole growth in fly embryos (Aydogan et al., 2020; Aydogan et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Aydogan et al., 2020 and Aydogan et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Plk4 oscillations persist to run even when the CCO is halted, and they continue to execute centriole formation independently of the cell cycle.
claims.source: Remarkably, Plk4 oscillations persist to run even when the CCO is halted, and they continue to execute centriole formation independently of the cell cycle (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is illustrated in Figure 2B and is stated in the text.

claims.claim: Oscillations of Plk4 at the centriole appear to be conserved in mammalian cells.
claims.source: Although such oscillations of Plk4 at the centriole appear to be conserved in mammalian cells (Takao et al., 2019), functionally orthologous mechanisms may regulate the formation of MTOCs in evolutionarily distant species, such as Mps1p kinase that governs the duplication of spindle pole bodies in budding yeast (Blank et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Takao et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Mps1p kinase governs the duplication of spindle pole bodies in budding yeast.
claims.source: Although such oscillations of Plk4 at the centriole appear to be conserved in mammalian cells (Takao et al., 2019), functionally orthologous mechanisms may regulate the formation of MTOCs in evolutionarily distant species, such as Mps1p kinase that governs the duplication of spindle pole bodies in budding yeast (Blank et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Blank et al., 2020.

claims.claim: The self-organizing nature of most mitotic spindles can waive the requirement for a functional centrosome in dividing cells.
claims.source: In fact, the self-organizing nature of most mitotic spindles can waive the requirement for a functional centrosome in dividing cells (Basto et al., 2006; Brugués and Needleman, 2014; Heald et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Basto et al., 2006; Brugués and Needleman, 2014; and Heald et al., 1996.

claims.claim: In the adult body where most cells are non-dividing, centriole biogenesis appears critical due to their function in templating different types of cilia.
claims.source: In the adult body where most cells are non-dividing, however, centriole biogenesis appears critical due to their function in templating different types of cilia (Basto et al., 2006), purposed for a variety of biological roles, such as the canonical part they play in mechano-chemical signal transduction (Singla and Reiter, 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Basto et al., 2006 and Singla and Reiter, 2006.

claims.claim: Cilia play a canonical part in mechano-chemical signal transduction.
claims.source: In the adult body where most cells are non-dividing, however, centriole biogenesis appears critical due to their function in templating different types of cilia (Basto et al., 2006), purposed for a variety of biological roles, such as the canonical part they play in mechano-chemical signal transduction (Singla and Reiter, 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Singla and Reiter, 2006.

claims.claim: Cilia are an essential component of the homeostatic program that regulates organismal health, particularly in respiratory, reproductive, and brain tissues where cells generate streams of vital fluids.
claims.source: Cilia are an equally essential component of the homeostatic program that regulates organismal health, particularly in respiratory, reproductive, and brain tissues where cells generate streams of vital fluids (Spassky and Meunier, 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Spassky and Meunier, 2017.

claims.claim: Tight regulation of centriole number is a chief determinant of cilia abundance in multi-ciliated cells.
claims.source: As these tissues are mostly composed of multi-ciliated cells, tight regulation of centriole number is a chief determinant of cilia abundance.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a logical inference from the composition of tissues.

claims.claim: Recent work on multi-ciliated airway epithelial cells highlights the physiological importance of ciliary abundance and Plk4's potential role in the homeostatic control of centriole numbers in non-dividing cells.
claims.source: Indeed, recent work on multi-ciliated airway epithelial cells highlights the physiological importance of ciliary abundance and Plk4's potential role in the homeostatic control of centriole numbers in these non-dividing cells (Nanjundappa et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nanjundappa et al., 2019.

claims.claim: In multi-ciliated neuron progenitors, Cdk1 is expressed at low levels that do not trigger mitosis, but is repurposed to pace certain steps of centriole biogenesis and cilia formation.
claims.source: Similarly, another recent study has demonstrated that, in multi-ciliated neuron progenitors, Cdk1 is expressed at low levels that do not trigger mitosis, but is repurposed to pace certain steps of centriole biogenesis and cilia formation (Al Jord et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Al Jord et al., 2017.

claims.claim: These findings collectively implicate a Cdk1-independent mechanism that drives centriole biogenesis in non-dividing cells, while regulating their numbers, at least partially, in a Plk4-dependent way.
claims.source: These findings collectively implicate a Cdk1-independent mechanism that drives centriole biogenesis in non-dividing cells, while regulating their numbers, at least partially, in a Plk4-dependent way.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as an inference from the collective findings discussed.

claims.claim: Cytoplasmic Plk4 levels often correlate with Plk4 levels on centrioles.
claims.source: Since cytoplasmic Plk4 levels often correlate with Plk4 levels on centrioles (Aydogan et al., 2020), an oscillatory expression of cytoplasmic Plk4 may guide the frequency and duration of centriolar Plk4 above an effective threshold (to trigger centriole biogenesis): the frequency of these integral durations may determine the number of rounds when centrioles can be produced, while the period spent above the effective enzymatic threshold may determine the size of centrioles (as depicted in Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Aydogan et al., 2020 and is illustrated in Figure 2.

claims.claim: An oscillatory expression of cytoplasmic Plk4 may guide the frequency and duration of centriolar Plk4 above an effective threshold to trigger centriole biogenesis.
claims.source: Since cytoplasmic Plk4 levels often correlate with Plk4 levels on centrioles (Aydogan et al., 2020), an oscillatory expression of cytoplasmic Plk4 may guide the frequency and duration of centriolar Plk4 above an effective threshold (to trigger centriole biogenesis): the frequency of these integral durations may determine the number of rounds when centrioles can be produced, while the period spent above the effective enzymatic threshold may determine the size of centrioles (as depicted in Figure 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a speculative hypothesis based on correlations and is illustrated in Figure 2.

claims.claim: In Cyanidioschyzon merolae, halting DNA replication stops the cycles of nuclei and cytokinesis, whereas chloroplast duplications continue to occur independently.
claims.source: Intriguingly in these red algae, halting DNA replication stops the cycles of nuclei and cytokinesis, whereas chloroplast duplications continue to occur independently (Itoh et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Itoh et al., 1996.

claims.claim: A study reports cyclic gene expression patterns during the chloroplast division cycles in C. merolae.
claims.source: Importantly, another study (Fujiwara et al., 2009) that reports cyclic gene expression patterns during the chloroplast division cycles in C. merolae provides other candidate cyclic genes, besides PLASTID DIVISION1 and 2, with which to further investigate the molecular basis of the autonomous chloroplast division cycles.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fujiwara et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Under lower temperatures, several events of the mitotic entry (such as nuclear envelope breakdown and chromosome condensation) occur without any detectable rise in the Cdk1 activity or cyclin B levels in early fly embryos.
claims.source: In this work, although a large range of changes in temperature (5–22°C) did not alter the order of major mitotic events, under lower temperatures several events of the mitotic entry (such as nuclear envelope breakdown and chromosome condensation) were observed to occur without any detectable rise in the Cdk1 activity or cyclin B levels.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as an observation from the work being discussed.

claims.claim: The segmentation clock can run independently of the cell cycle during development.
claims.source: Until recently, studies on developmental timing have helped to reveal only a few autonomous timing mechanisms unequivocally, most notably the segmentation clock (Palmeirim et al., 1997) and the timer that controls the clonal development and differentiation of oligodendrocytes (Temple and Raff, 1986), both of whom can run independently of the cell cycle during development (Gao et al., 1997; Zhang et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Palmeirim et al., 1997; Gao et al., 1997; and Zhang et al., 2008.

claims.claim: The timer that controls the clonal development and differentiation of oligodendrocytes can run independently of the cell cycle during development.
claims.source: Until recently, studies on developmental timing have helped to reveal only a few autonomous timing mechanisms unequivocally, most notably the segmentation clock (Palmeirim et al., 1997) and the timer that controls the clonal development and differentiation of oligodendrocytes (Temple and Raff, 1986), both of whom can run independently of the cell cycle during development (Gao et al., 1997; Zhang et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Temple and Raff, 1986; Gao et al., 1997; and Zhang et al., 2008.

claims.claim: After 14 rounds of synchronous nuclear divisions in the syncytium, thousands of nuclei rapidly become encapsulated by membrane and cellularize within the blastoderm during fly development.
claims.source: MBT during fly development appears to be no exception: after 14 rounds of synchronous nuclear divisions in the syncytium, thousands of nuclei rapidly become encapsulated by membrane and cellularize within the blastoderm (Farrell and O'Farrell, 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Farrell and O'Farrell, 2014.

claims.claim: The fly embryo appears to start degrading its maternally provided RNA and simultaneously begins expressing the majority of its zygotic genes during mid-blastula transition.
claims.source: Meanwhile, the fly embryo appears to start degrading its maternally provided RNA and simultaneously begins expressing the majority of its zygotic genes (Tadros and Lipshitz, 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tadros and Lipshitz, 2009.

claims.claim: The major temporal trigger of maternal-to-zygotic transition and its associated events has long been assumed to be the exponential increase in nuclear-to-cytoplasmic (N/C) ratio as a function of cell cycle progression.
claims.source: The major temporal trigger of maternal-to-zygotic transition and its associated events – both in flies and other species – has long been assumed to be the exponential increase in nuclear-to-cytoplasmic (N/C) ratio as a function of cell cycle progression (Edgar et al., 1986; Newport and Kirschner, 1982).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Edgar et al., 1986 and Newport and Kirschner, 1982.

claims.claim: Neither the activation of zygotic genome nor the timing of cellularization is governed by an accurate N/C ratio or cell cycle progression in fly embryos.
claims.source: With elegant experiments that genetically perturb the progression of cell cycle in fly embryos, recent work suggests the contrary: neither the activation of zygotic genome nor the timing of cellularization is governed by an accurate N/C ratio or cell cycle progression, and both events appear to occur when the nuclear divisions are halted 2–3 rounds in prior (Figure 3A; McCleland and O'Farrell, 2008; Strong et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McCleland and O'Farrell, 2008 and Strong et al., 2020, and is illustrated in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Both zygotic genome activation and cellularization appear to occur when the nuclear divisions are halted 2–3 rounds in prior in fly embryos.
claims.source: With elegant experiments that genetically perturb the progression of cell cycle in fly embryos, recent work suggests the contrary: neither the activation of zygotic genome nor the timing of cellularization is governed by an accurate N/C ratio or cell cycle progression, and both events appear to occur when the nuclear divisions are halted 2–3 rounds in prior (Figure 3A; McCleland and O'Farrell, 2008; Strong et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McCleland and O'Farrell, 2008 and Strong et al., 2020, and is illustrated in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The timing of cellularization remains relatively similar to wild-type conditions in arrested embryos, eliminating the possibility that a mere slowing in nuclear cycles could elicit the trigger of cellularization.
claims.source: Although the slowing of cell cycle progression (in arrested embryos) could explain the premature trigger of zygotic genome activation independently of a set N/C ratio (Strong et al., 2020), the timing of cellularization remains relatively similar to wild-type conditions, eliminating the possibility that a mere slowing in nuclear cycles could elicit the trigger of cellularization.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as an observation that eliminates a hypothesis.

claims.claim: These findings hint at a potential autonomous timing mechanism responsible for the onset of cellularization.
claims.source: These findings hint at a potential autonomous timing mechanism responsible for the onset of this hallmark morphological event.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as an inference from the findings discussed.

claims.claim: Cortex contractions in the unfertilized eggs of various vertebrate and invertebrate species occur in periodic cycles that are independent of any cell cycle progression.
claims.source: Though speculative, a potential mechanism could relate to a series of seminal observations regarding cortex contractions in the unfertilized eggs of various vertebrate and invertebrate species, occurring in periodic cycles that are independent of any cell cycle progression (Ciemerych, 1995; Hara et al., 1980; Shinagawa, 1983; Waksmundzka et al., 1984; Yoneda et al., 1982).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ciemerych, 1995; Hara et al., 1980; Shinagawa, 1983; Waksmundzka et al., 1984; and Yoneda et al., 1982.

claims.claim: Cortex contractions are intimately linked to actomyosin-dependent shrinking and stretching of the embryonal membrane.
claims.source: Just as cellularization (Schmidt and Grosshans, 2018), the cortex contractions are intimately linked to actomyosin-dependent shrinking and stretching of the embryonal membrane (Chugh and Paluch, 2018), and could potentially count a (right) number of pre-ZGA membrane cleavages that must occur prior to cellularization.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schmidt and Grosshans, 2018 and Chugh and Paluch, 2018.

claims.claim: Previous studies have identified a series of zygotic factors that are required for the proper completion of cellularization (both structurally and temporally).
claims.source: Indeed, previous studies have identified a series of zygotic factors that are required for the proper completion of cellularization (both structurally and temporally) (Vastenhouw et al., 2019), but to the best of our knowledge, none of these could elicit an embryonic response that can completely halt the initial trigger of cellularization.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vastenhouw et al., 2019.

claims.claim: A recent work has revealed the molecular basis of a long-suspected developmental clock that triggers apicobasal cell polarization independently of cell cycle progression in mice embryos.
claims.source: Although our piece particularly focuses on aspects of timing in de novo cellularization, similar questions on cell cycle autonomous timing can be proposed for other morphogenesis phenomena in early development. Indeed, a recent work has revealed the molecular basis of a long-suspected developmental clock that triggers apicobasal cell polarization independently of cell cycle progression in mice embryos (Zhu et al., 2020; Figure 3B), strongly supporting the possibility of other autonomous timing mechanisms in development and morphogenesis.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhu et al., 2020 and is illustrated in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Metabolic regulation can be periodic and autonomously regulated.
claims.source: Evidence that metabolic regulation can be periodic and autonomously regulated (Papagiannakis et al., 2017; Slavov et al., 2011; Benjamin et al., 2005) (i.e., the metabolic cycles) had therefore opened an alternative avenue in this endeavor.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Papagiannakis et al., 2017; Slavov et al., 2011; and Benjamin et al., 2005.

claims.claim: Metabolic cycles appear to be analogously conserved across species in different branches of the phylogenetic tree.
claims.source: Recent research has demonstrated that, similar to the circadian clock (Dunlap and Loros, 2017), metabolic cycles appear to be analogously conserved across species in different branches of the phylogenetic tree; but unlike the circadian clock, the period of metabolic cycles does not appear to be set universally among different organisms (Benjamin et al., 2005; Zhu et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dunlap and Loros, 2017; Benjamin et al., 2005; and Zhu et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The period of metabolic cycles does not appear to be set universally among different organisms.
claims.source: Recent research has demonstrated that, similar to the circadian clock (Dunlap and Loros, 2017), metabolic cycles appear to be analogously conserved across species in different branches of the phylogenetic tree; but unlike the circadian clock, the period of metabolic cycles does not appear to be set universally among different organisms (Benjamin et al., 2005; Zhu et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Benjamin et al., 2005 and Zhu et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Pioneering efforts in generating robust statistical methods enabled the discovery of 8 and 12 hr transcriptional rhythms in mice hepatocytes.
claims.source: Pioneering efforts in generating robust statistical methods to study non-circadian periods with low false-discovery rates enabled the discovery of 8 and 12 hr transcriptional rhythms in mice hepatocytes (Cretenet et al., 2010; Hughes et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cretenet et al., 2010 and Hughes et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Products of 8 or 12 hr expressing genes appear to regulate different cellular processes, from protein processing to lipid metabolism, in liver cells.
claims.source: Products of such 8 or 12 hr expressing genes appear to regulate different cellular processes, from protein processing to lipid metabolism, in liver cells (Hughes et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hughes et al., 2009.

claims.claim: The ~8 and ~12 hr transcriptional rhythms found in cells extracted from living mice cannot be recapitulated using their cultured counterparts.
claims.source: Several lines of initial evidence suggested that the ~8 and ~12 hr transcriptional rhythms, which were found in cells extracted from living mice, cannot be recapitulated using their cultured counterparts, implying that they might indeed be by-products of systemic signals such as feeding cues (Cretenet et al., 2010; Hughes et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cretenet et al., 2010 and Hughes et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Perturbing several major components in the negative arm of the circadian clock (e.g., Cry1/Cry2) demonstrates a significant dampening in the amplitude of 12 hr transcriptional oscillations.
claims.source: Furthermore, with experiments that perturbed several major components in the negative arm of the circadian clock (e.g., Cry1/Cry2), a study demonstrated a significant dampening in the amplitude of 12 hr transcriptional oscillations, indicating that these rhythms must be generated, at least in part, by a circadian clock (and/or a feeding cue)-dependent mechanism (Cretenet et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cretenet et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Recent studies can recapitulate the 12 hr transcriptional rhythms both in synchronized and unsynchronized hepatic cells.
claims.source: In stark contrast to previous work, this new heave-ho that brings a methodological twist to the field can recapitulate the 12 hr transcriptional rhythms both in synchronized and unsynchronized hepatic cells – the latter eliminating confounding entrainment effects by the circadian clock (e.g., by tunicamycin incubation) or feeding cues (such as via serum deprivation).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a result from recent studies using new methodological approaches.

claims.claim: The majority of 12 hr rhythmic transcriptome in mouse liver is expressed independently of the circadian clock.
claims.source: Importantly, this stream of work also indicates that the majority of 12 hr rhythmic transcriptome in mouse liver is expressed independently of the circadian clock (Pan et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pan et al., 2020 and Zhu et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The biological role of 12 hr transcriptional oscillations points to the spatiotemporal control of central dogma, from gene expression to protein folding.
claims.source: Although the biological role of 12 hr transcriptional oscillations remains unclear, current evidence – given the nature of the genes involved – points to the spatiotemporal control of central dogma, from gene expression to protein folding.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as an inference from current evidence.

claims.claim: 12 hr transcriptional oscillations involve the stress-mediated regulation of gene expression via IRE1α and XBP1.
claims.source: This particularly involves the stress-mediated regulation of gene expression via IRE1α (Cretenet et al., 2010), a stress sensor on the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), and XBP1 (Pan et al., 2020), the transcriptional regulator of unfolded protein response (Walter and Ron, 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cretenet et al., 2010; Pan et al., 2020; and Walter and Ron, 2011.

claims.claim: IRE1α is a stress sensor on the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
claims.source: This particularly involves the stress-mediated regulation of gene expression via IRE1α (Cretenet et al., 2010), a stress sensor on the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), and XBP1 (Pan et al., 2020), the transcriptional regulator of unfolded protein response (Walter and Ron, 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge.

claims.claim: XBP1 is the transcriptional regulator of unfolded protein response.
claims.source: This particularly involves the stress-mediated regulation of gene expression via IRE1α (Cretenet et al., 2010), a stress sensor on the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), and XBP1 (Pan et al., 2020), the transcriptional regulator of unfolded protein response (Walter and Ron, 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Walter and Ron, 2011.

claims.claim: In 1962, Herbert Simon postulated the theory that most complex networks must take the form of hierarchy with unifying properties that are independent of their specific content.
claims.source: In 1962, Nobel laureate Herbert Simon wrote his pioneering article The Architecture of Complexity, postulating the theory that most complex networks (from individual decision-making processes to forming societies) must take the form of hierarchy with unifying properties that are independent of their specific content (Simon, 1962).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Simon, 1962.

claims.claim: One emergent property in most complex networks is to acquire numerous nodes that represent subdivisions and to rapidly evolve to interconnect these subunits for robustness.
claims.source: One such 'emergent' property in most complex networks is to acquire numerous nodes that represent subdivisions and to rapidly evolve to interconnect these subunits for robustness.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a general principle of complex networks.

claims.claim: DNA replication and spindle formation are processes that can operate freely in parallel.
claims.source: For example, although DNA replication and spindle formation are processes that can operate freely in parallel (Hartwell, 1974), they are 'latched' to occur once and only once in every cell division.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hartwell, 1974.

claims.claim: Cycles of DNA replication can occur in the absence of nuclear divisions (e.g., the Gnu mutants in fly embryos).
claims.source: It has been long known that cycles of DNA replication can occur in the absence of nuclear divisions (e.g., the Gnu mutants in fly embryos; Freeman et al., 1986), and recent studies on fly development argue that this phenomenon is neither unique to the embryonic tissue nor is a consequence of artificial genetic alteration: multiple rounds of DNA replication not only can occur naturally in the absence of mitosis (Zielke et al., 2011), but also can serve as part of the tissue repair program in various adult tissues (Box et al., 2019; Cohen et al., 2018) – also eliminating the possibility that these autonomous cycles are just an artifact of evolution (i.e., the Darwinian requirement for the utility of intermediate forms; Darwin, 1909).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Freeman et al., 1986; Zielke et al., 2011; Box et al., 2019; Cohen et al., 2018; and Darwin, 1909.

claims.claim: Multiple rounds of DNA replication can occur naturally in the absence of mitosis.
claims.source: It has been long known that cycles of DNA replication can occur in the absence of nuclear divisions (e.g., the Gnu mutants in fly embryos; Freeman et al., 1986), and recent studies on fly development argue that this phenomenon is neither unique to the embryonic tissue nor is a consequence of artificial genetic alteration: multiple rounds of DNA replication not only can occur naturally in the absence of mitosis (Zielke et al., 2011), but also can serve as part of the tissue repair program in various adult tissues (Box et al., 2019; Cohen et al., 2018) – also eliminating the possibility that these autonomous cycles are just an artifact of evolution (i.e., the Darwinian requirement for the utility of intermediate forms; Darwin, 1909).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zielke et al., 2011; Box et al., 2019; and Cohen et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Multiple rounds of DNA replication can serve as part of the tissue repair program in various adult tissues.
claims.source: It has been long known that cycles of DNA replication can occur in the absence of nuclear divisions (e.g., the Gnu mutants in fly embryos; Freeman et al., 1986), and recent studies on fly development argue that this phenomenon is neither unique to the embryonic tissue nor is a consequence of artificial genetic alteration: multiple rounds of DNA replication not only can occur naturally in the absence of mitosis (Zielke et al., 2011), but also can serve as part of the tissue repair program in various adult tissues (Box et al., 2019; Cohen et al., 2018) – also eliminating the possibility that these autonomous cycles are just an artifact of evolution (i.e., the Darwinian requirement for the utility of intermediate forms; Darwin, 1909).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Box et al., 2019 and Cohen et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Sustained rounds of DNA replication that skew stable cells in favor of polyploidy take up roles in tissue repair during mammalian development.
claims.source: Such sustained rounds of DNA replication that skew stable cells in favor of polyploidy similarly take up on roles in tissue repair during mammalian development as well (Porrello et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Porrello et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Polyploidy in most proliferating mammalian cells often occur as an unwanted consequence of DNA damage or due to defects in chromosome segregation.
claims.source: However, polyploidy in most proliferating mammalian cells often occur as an unwanted consequence of DNA damage or due to defects in chromosome segregation (Chow and Poon, 2010) and, unlike in fly endocycling cells (Zhang et al., 2014a), leads to p53-mediated cell death.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chow and Poon, 2010 and Zhang et al., 2014a.

claims.claim: Polyploidy in proliferating mammalian cells leads to p53-mediated cell death.
claims.source: However, polyploidy in most proliferating mammalian cells often occur as an unwanted consequence of DNA damage or due to defects in chromosome segregation (Chow and Poon, 2010) and, unlike in fly endocycling cells (Zhang et al., 2014a), leads to p53-mediated cell death.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge.

claims.claim: Cells that undergo terminal differentiation may experience a significant decline in p53 levels.
claims.source: One idea that can explain this discrepancy is that, although majority of the mammalian proliferating cells maintain high levels of p53 expression, cells that undergo terminal differentiation may experience a significant decline in p53 levels (Tedeschi and Di Giovanni, 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tedeschi and Di Giovanni, 2009.

claims.claim: Post-translational regulation of protein stability has emerged as a prominent target for an oscillator to couple another one.
claims.source: Although there are a number of ways and conditions that help phase-locking two or more biological cycles (Heltberg et al., 2021), post-translational regulation of protein stability has emerged as a prominent target for an oscillator to couple another one.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as an emerging concept and is supported by a citation to Heltberg et al., 2021.

claims.claim: The enzymatic ability to induce protein modifications (e.g., phosphorylation) with varying levels of potency and efficacy may elucidate how cell-cycle-driven proteolytic activities could couple cycles of cell divisions to peripheral biological cycles that are otherwise autonomous.
claims.source: In this realm, the enzymatic ability to induce protein modifications (e.g., phosphorylation) with varying levels of potency and efficacy (Holt et al., 2009; Swaffer et al., 2018; Swaffer et al., 2016; Ubersax et al., 2003) may elucidate how cell-cycle-driven proteolytic activities could couple cycles of cell divisions to peripheral biological cycles that are otherwise autonomous.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Holt et al., 2009; Swaffer et al., 2018; Swaffer et al., 2016; and Ubersax et al., 2003.

claims.claim: The clock of centriole biogenesis in fly embryos appears to be phase-locked to the cell cycle by a molecular mechanism that is in mitosis.
claims.source: The clock of centriole biogenesis in fly embryos, for example, appears to be phase-locked to the cell cycle by a molecular mechanism that is – expectedly – in mitosis (Aydogan et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Aydogan et al., 2020.

results.result: The manuscript defines terminology for 'clocks' in the circadian field versus the emerging concept of 'autonomous clocks', establishing that circadian clocks have strict criteria (free-running, entrainment, temperature compensation) while autonomous clocks use 'clock' as an umbrella term for timing mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C2 are well-supported by citations to established literature. C1 provides the traditional circadian definition with multiple references, while C2 introduces the broader autonomous clock concept with appropriate citation. These definitional claims establish the conceptual framework for the review.

results.result: The manuscript traces the historical development of cell cycle nomenclature and models, from Howard and Pelc's 1953 naming of cell cycle phases based on chromosome dynamics, through the 'ratchet' model where the CCO acts as a master clock, to the emerging alternative hypothesis that the CCO phase-locks a network of local autonomous oscillators.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C7 provide a coherent historical narrative supported by appropriate citations. The progression from historical nomenclature (C3-C4) through the prevailing model (C5-C6) to the alternative hypothesis (C7) is well-documented with references to Nasmyth 1996, Stern and Nurse 1996, Alberts et al. 2002, Lu and Cross 2010, and Morgan 2010.

results.result: The phase-locking hypothesis was based on observations that Cdc14 oscillations in budding yeast continue when the CCO is halted, though perturbing the CCO stops cell divisions, representing a conceptual advance in understanding how autonomous clocks can be coordinated.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C10 are supported by citations to Lu and Cross 2010 and Morgan 2010. The observations about Cdc14 oscillations (C8), the consequence of CCO perturbation (C9), and the conceptual significance (C10) form a logical progression that establishes the foundation for the phase-locking hypothesis.

results.result: The pre-mid blastula Drosophila embryo serves as a powerful system for studying autonomous clocks because circadian clock components are not expressed until later stages. In this system, an organelle clock regulates centriole formation through oscillatory Plk4 localization that determines enzymatic thresholds for centriole biogenesis, provides homeostasis for centriole growth, and can run autonomously when the cell cycle is halted.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C20 present a well-supported major finding with multiple citations (Aydogan et al. 2020, 2018, 2021; Yuan et al. 2016; Yadav et al. 2014). The system justification (C11-C12), the discovery of the organelle clock (C13), background on centrioles and Plk4 (C14-C17), and the key findings about Plk4 oscillations (C18-C20) are all supported by appropriate references and illustrated in Figure 2.

results.result: Plk4 oscillations at centrioles appear conserved in mammalian cells, and functionally orthologous mechanisms like Mps1p kinase regulate MTOC formation in evolutionarily distant species like budding yeast.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C22 are supported by citations to Takao et al. 2019 and Blank et al. 2020, demonstrating evolutionary conservation and functional analogy of the centriole clock mechanism across species.

results.result: While centrosomes are dispensable for mitotic spindle formation in dividing cells, centriole biogenesis is critical in non-dividing adult cells for templating cilia that play essential roles in mechano-chemical signaling and tissue homeostasis. Recent work demonstrates that Cdk1 can pace centriole biogenesis in multi-ciliated cells at low levels that don't trigger mitosis, and that centriole biogenesis can continue when Cdk1 is inhibited, implicating a Cdk1-independent, Plk4-dependent mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C29 and C31 are well-supported by multiple citations (Basto et al. 2006, Heald et al. 1996, Singla and Reiter 2006, Spassky and Meunier 2017, Nanjundappa et al. 2019, Al Jord et al. 2017). The progression from dispensability in dividing cells to importance in non-dividing cells, and the evidence for Cdk1-independent mechanisms, forms a coherent argument.

results.result: Cytoplasmic Plk4 levels correlate with centriolar Plk4 levels, and oscillatory expression of cytoplasmic Plk4 may guide the frequency and duration of centriolar Plk4 above an effective threshold to control centriole number and size.
results.evaluation: Claim C32 is supported by citation to Aydogan et al. 2020, but C33 is explicitly speculative ('may guide'). While the hypothesis is illustrated in Figure 2 and builds logically on C32, it lacks direct experimental validation and is presented as a potential mechanism requiring future investigation.

results.result: In the red alga Cyanidioschyzon merolae, halting DNA replication stops nuclear and cytokinesis cycles while chloroplast duplications continue independently, and cyclic gene expression patterns during chloroplast division have been identified.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C35 are supported by citations to Itoh et al. 1996 and Fujiwara et al. 2009. These findings provide evidence for autonomous organelle division cycles in a different system, supporting the broader concept of autonomous clocks.

results.result: Under lower temperatures in early fly embryos, mitotic entry events like nuclear envelope breakdown and chromosome condensation occur without detectable rises in Cdk1 activity or cyclin B levels.
results.evaluation: Claim C36 is supported by observations from Falahati et al. 2021 (implied from context). This finding challenges the traditional view that Cdk1 activity directly triggers all mitotic events and supports the existence of autonomous timing mechanisms.

results.result: The segmentation clock and the timer controlling oligodendrocyte development are autonomous timing mechanisms that can run independently of the cell cycle during development.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C38 are well-supported by multiple citations (Palmeirim et al. 1997, Temple and Raff 1986, Gao et al. 1997, Zhang et al. 2008). These represent established examples of cell cycle-independent developmental timing mechanisms.

results.result: During Drosophila mid-blastula transition, neither zygotic genome activation nor cellularization timing is governed by accurate N/C ratio or cell cycle progression as traditionally assumed. Both events occur when nuclear divisions are halted 2-3 rounds prior, with cellularization timing remaining similar to wild-type in arrested embryos, suggesting a potential autonomous timing mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C45 present a coherent challenge to the traditional N/C ratio model, supported by citations to Farrell and O'Farrell 2014, Tadros and Lipshitz 2009, Edgar et al. 1986, Newport and Kirschner 1982, McCleland and O'Farrell 2008, and Strong et al. 2020. The evidence is illustrated in Figure 3A. The inference of an autonomous timing mechanism (C45) follows logically from the observations.

results.result: Cortex contractions in unfertilized eggs occur in periodic cycles independent of cell cycle progression and are linked to actomyosin-dependent membrane dynamics. While zygotic factors are required for proper cellularization completion, none can completely halt its initial trigger.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C47 are supported by multiple citations (Ciemerych 1995, Hara et al. 1980, Shinagawa 1983, Waksmundzka et al. 1984, Yoneda et al. 1982, Schmidt and Grosshans 2018, Chugh and Paluch 2018), but the connection to cellularization timing is explicitly speculative. C48 is supported by Vastenhouw et al. 2019 but the negative result (inability to halt cellularization) may reflect incomplete investigation rather than definitive evidence.

results.result: A developmental clock triggering apicobasal cell polarization independently of cell cycle progression has been identified in mouse embryos.
results.evaluation: Claim C49 is supported by citation to Zhu et al. 2020 and illustrated in Figure 3B. This represents another example of an autonomous developmental timing mechanism.

results.result: Metabolic regulation can be periodic and autonomously regulated (metabolic cycles), which are analogously conserved across species but with periods that are not universally set among organisms, unlike the circadian clock.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C52 are supported by citations to Papagiannakis et al. 2017, Slavov et al. 2011, Benjamin et al. 2005, Dunlap and Loros 2017, and Zhu et al. 2017. These establish metabolic cycles as another class of autonomous timing mechanisms.

results.result: Statistical methods enabled discovery of 8 and 12 hr transcriptional rhythms in mouse hepatocytes that regulate various cellular processes. Initial evidence suggested these rhythms cannot be recapitulated in cultured cells and are dampened by perturbing circadian clock components, implying dependence on systemic signals and/or the circadian clock.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C56 are supported by citations to Cretenet et al. 2010 and Hughes et al. 2009. These findings represent the initial characterization of ultradian transcriptional rhythms, though later work (discussed in subsequent claims) challenges some of these conclusions.

results.result: Recent studies using new methodological approaches can recapitulate 12 hr transcriptional rhythms in both synchronized and unsynchronized hepatic cells, demonstrating that the majority of 12 hr rhythmic transcriptome is expressed independently of the circadian clock. These oscillations involve stress-mediated gene expression regulation via IRE1α and XBP1, pointing to spatiotemporal control of gene expression and protein folding.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C62 are supported by citations to Pan et al. 2020, Zhu et al. 2017, Cretenet et al. 2010, and Walter and Ron 2011. These findings represent a major revision of the earlier understanding (C55-C56) and provide evidence for autonomous 12 hr transcriptional rhythms with specific molecular mechanisms.

results.result: Herbert Simon's 1962 theory posited that complex networks take hierarchical forms with unifying properties independent of content, with an emergent property being the acquisition of numerous subdivisions that interconnect for robustness.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C64 are supported by citation to Simon 1962. This provides theoretical framework for understanding biological timing networks as complex hierarchical systems.

results.result: DNA replication and spindle formation can operate in parallel but are normally phase-locked. DNA replication cycles can occur without nuclear divisions in various contexts including Gnu mutants, naturally in the absence of mitosis, and as part of tissue repair programs in adult tissues, serving physiological functions in both fly and mammalian development.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C69 are supported by multiple citations (Hartwell 1974, Freeman et al. 1986, Zielke et al. 2011, Box et al. 2019, Cohen et al. 2018, Darwin 1909, Porrello et al. 2011). These demonstrate that autonomous DNA replication cycles are not artifacts but have evolved functions.

results.result: Polyploidy in proliferating mammalian cells typically results from DNA damage or segregation defects and leads to p53-mediated cell death, but terminally differentiated cells may tolerate polyploidy due to declining p53 levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C71 are supported by citations (Chow and Poon 2010, Zhang et al. 2014a), but C72 is explicitly presented as a speculative idea ('One idea that can explain') with only one supporting citation (Tedeschi and Di Giovanni 2009). The mechanism explaining differential polyploidy tolerance requires further validation.

results.result: Post-translational regulation of protein stability has emerged as a prominent mechanism for phase-locking between oscillators, with enzymatic modifications of varying potency and efficacy potentially explaining how cell-cycle-driven proteolytic activities couple to autonomous biological cycles.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C74 are supported by citations to Heltberg et al. 2021, Holt et al. 2009, Swaffer et al. 2018, 2016, and Ubersax et al. 2003. This identifies a key molecular mechanism for coordinating autonomous clocks.

results.result: The centriole biogenesis clock in fly embryos is phase-locked to the cell cycle through mitotic mechanisms, but acquires additional interphase coupling by the 13th nuclear division when Wee1 slows the cell cycle. Wee1-deficient embryos lose robustness in interphase coupling of the centriole cycle.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C78 are supported by citations to Aydogan et al. 2020 and Stumpff et al. 2004, with illustration in Figure 4. This demonstrates developmental regulation of phase-locking strength and identifies Wee1 as a key coupling factor.

results.result: The circadian clock and cell cycle are phase-locked at a 1:1 ratio through bidirectional coupling: Wee1's circadian expression couples the cell cycle to the circadian clock, while Cdk1 couples the circadian clock to the cell cycle via REV-ERBα phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C81 are supported by citations to Bieler et al. 2014, Yan and Goldbeter 2019, Matsuo et al. 2003, and Zhao et al. 2016, with illustration in Figure 4. This demonstrates reciprocal phase-locking between major temporal networks.

results.result: The mitochondrial fission enzyme Drp1 can be coupled to both the cell cycle and circadian clock through different phosphorylation mechanisms: Cdk1 phosphorylation at Ser616 activates it, while dephosphorylation at Ser637 by the circadian-regulated phosphatase calcineurin also activates it.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C85 are supported by citations to Taguchi et al. 2007, Schmitt et al. 2018, and Cereghetti et al. 2008, with illustration in Figure 4. This demonstrates how a single substrate can be regulated by multiple temporal networks.

results.result: Daughter centrioles require two cell cycles to mature into functional centrosomes (1:2 phase-locking). Deviations from this ratio cause pathological consequences: ratios <1:2 produce monopolar spindles, while ratios >1:2 produce multipolar spindles, both leading to aneuploidy.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C87 are supported by citations to Palazzo et al. 1999, Compton 2011, Godinho and Pellman 2014, and Hinchcliffe 2011. This demonstrates the physiological importance of maintaining specific phase-locking ratios.

results.result: Both 1:1 and 1:2 phase-locking ratios between circadian clock and cell cycle can coexist in the same cell population, with cells coupling every ~24 hr to either one or half a division cycle. This occurs because increasing locking strength increases the span of coupling for different p:q ratios, leading to overlaps.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C90 are supported by citations to Droin et al. 2019 and Heltberg et al. 2021. This demonstrates flexibility in phase-locking relationships and provides theoretical explanation via Arnold Tongues.

results.result: Several studies challenge the necessity of transcription-translation feedback loops (TTFLs) for running circadian clocks, including observations of circadian redox rhythms in enucleated red blood cells. The bifunctional kinase/phosphatase nature of KaiC ATPase is necessary and sufficient for autonomous operation of the cyanobacterial circadian clock.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C93 are supported by citations to Putker et al. 2021, Lipton et al. 2015, Nakajima et al. 2005, Tomita et al. 2005, O'Neill and Reddy 2011, and Terauchi et al. 2007. These findings challenge the TTFL paradigm and identify protein-level mechanisms as sufficient for autonomous oscillations.

results.result: Plk4's autokinase activity may contribute to autonomous centriole clock operation through recruitment to centrioles promoting both inhibitory receptor phosphorylation and autophosphorylation in trans that triggers ubiquitylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C95 are supported by citations to Aydogan et al. 2020, Boese et al. 2018, Cunha-Ferreira et al. 2013, Guderian et al. 2010, Holland et al. 2010, and Rogers et al. 2009. This proposes a molecular mechanism for autonomous clock operation via autoregulatory feedback.

results.result: PKC is a suicide enzyme whose autophosphorylation facilitates both activation and degradation. PKC acts as a master switch for lysosome biogenesis independently of mTOR signaling. While PKC-mediated lysosome biogenesis is coupled to the cell cycle by CDK4/6, halting cell cycle progression does not prevent further lysosome biogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C99 are supported by citations to Feng and Hannun 1998, Gould and Newton 2008, Li et al. 2016, and Yin et al. 2020. This identifies PKC as another potential autonomous clock mechanism and demonstrates cell cycle-independent organelle biogenesis.

results.result: The volume of residue 402 on KaiC dodecamers strongly influences the KaiABC oscillator period in a negative correlation (bulkier residue = shorter period), with tryptophan variants producing <24 hr periods and alanine variants producing ~5 day periods.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C102 are supported by citation to Ito-Miwa et al. 2020 and illustrated in Figure 5. This demonstrates how single amino acid changes can dramatically tune oscillator period, providing insights into clock mechanisms.

results.result: The period of p53 oscillations varies between species due to differing p53 degradation rates (~3 hr in rodents vs ~6 hr in primates). Protein stability differences between rodents and primates occur globally, not just for p53. The segmentation clock similarly runs twice as fast in mice (~3 hr) compared to humans (~6 hr).
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C107 are supported by citations to Stewart-Ornstein and Lahav 2017, Matsuda et al. 2020, and Rayon et al. 2020. This demonstrates that emergent chemical properties like protein stability can influence oscillator periods across species.

results.result: Yeast metabolic cycles (YMC) involve periodic expression of three gene superclusters temporally compartmentalizing oxidative and reductive stages. Reductive stages promote mitochondrial biogenesis followed by vacuole biogenesis for waste degradation. YMCs occur at 4-5 hr periods, ~3× longer than cell cycles and ~5× shorter than circadian rhythms.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C110 are supported by citation to Benjamin et al. 2005. The period comparison (C110) provides strong evidence for temporal autonomy of YMCs from both cell cycle and circadian rhythms.

results.result: In budding yeast, ~70% of genes transcribed cyclically during cell division can continue periodic expression without robust cell cycle progression. Sic1 provides a mechanism promoting nuclear divisions when mitotic cyclin levels are low.
results.evaluation: Claim C111 is supported by Orlando et al. 2008, but the manuscript notes lack of strict consensus on this finding and that periodic transcription in arrested cells may not be as global as originally proposed. C112 is supported by Rahi et al. 2016 and provides functional insight, but the overall extent and significance of autonomous transcription cycles remains debated.

results.result: Under high glucose conditions in yeast, more transcripts display oscillatory expression, enriched for metabolic functions. The authors propose this helps satisfy homeostatic demands. However, in vitro evolution experiments show cyclic behavior can emerge without cyclic cues, suggesting oscillatory expression might be an emergent property that is suppressed under low glucose.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C114 describe observations from Wang et al. 2015 (implied), but the 'energy-conservation' interpretation is explicitly noted as requiring direct causal testing. C115 (supported by Wildenberg and Murray 2014) provides an alternative interpretation. The functional significance remains unclear.

results.result: Plasmodium infection causes cyclic symptoms every ~24 or 48 hr. Recent studies demonstrate that while the intraerythrocytic developmental cycle can be entrained by host cues, it is likely run by an autonomous clock regulating transcriptional cycles that operate independently of the cell cycle and/or circadian clock.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C117 are supported by citations to Hawking et al. 1968, Rijo-Ferreira et al. 2020, and Smith et al. 2020. This identifies an autonomous clock in a pathogenic organism with potential medical relevance.

results.result: Pathogenic organisms form membrane-bound inclusions to protect from host responses. During endosymbiosis, horizontal gene transfer helped hosts control organelle divisions. Parasitic inclusions have been conceptualized as de novo organelles that may regulate their own developmental cycles.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C119 are supported by citations to Moore and Ouellette 2014 and Husnik and McCutcheon 2018. However, C120 is explicitly speculative ('may regulate') and the temporal regulation of these cycles is acknowledged as currently unknown.

results.result: The degree of phase-locking by cell cycle and circadian clock affects autonomous clock identification: stronger phase-locking makes intrinsic rhythms more likely to be evolutionarily redundant. Almost 50% of mouse genes show circadian expression in at least one organ, while only 10% do in deep-sea Bathymodiolus azoricus, illustrating differential phase-locking strength.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C123 are supported by citations to Lu and Cross 2010, Morgan 2010, Zhang et al. 2014b, and Mat et al. 2020. This provides important methodological insight for identifying autonomous clocks and demonstrates environmental influence on phase-locking strength.

results.result: Mammalian cells cannot tolerate prolonged mitotic arrest and activate p53-dependent apoptosis, while yeast uses a single Cdk versus mammalian double-digit Cdks. Yeast has been a hotbed for phenomena occurring periodically in arrested cells, including free-running budding cycles and CO2 production rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C126 are supported by citations to Chen 2016, Malumbres 2014, Haase and Reed 1999, and Novak and Mitchison 1986. This explains why yeast is a more tractable system for studying autonomous clocks.

results.result: Cultured human cells show potentially autonomous growth rate oscillations (~4 hr period, a sixth subharmonic of circadian period) that continue in S-phase-arrested cultures. Rapamycin partially dictates the period, indicating mTOR involvement. mTOR activity is a target of the circadian clock protein Per2.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C130 are supported by Liu et al. 2020, demonstrating cell cycle-independent oscillations. However, C131 (supported by Wu et al. 2019) suggests potential circadian clock involvement, making the 'autonomy' uncertain. The manuscript acknowledges these oscillations require further investigation of biological function and relevance.

results.result: A microfluidics system enables tracking individual bacteria for tens of generations under controlled conditions, successfully identifying synthetic gene oscillators with up to 30-fold period differences.
results.evaluation: Claim C132 is supported by citation to Luro et al. 2020. This demonstrates technological approaches for identifying autonomous clocks at single-cell resolution.
